rows.stem:
(a) Name any two materials other than hydrogen that can be used as fuel in fuel cells.
(b) Define molar conductivity.
rows.solution:
(a) Methane and methanol. Any combustible fuel that can be oxidised at an electrode will serve — methane, methanol, ethanol and carbon monoxide are all used. The defining feature of a fuel cell is that the reactants are supplied continuously from outside rather than stored inside, so it runs as long as the fuel is fed.

(b) Molar conductivity of a solution at a given concentration is the conductance of the volume \(V\) of solution containing ONE MOLE of electrolyte, held between two electrodes of cross-sectional area \(A\) and one unit length apart. In symbols,
\(\Lambda_m = \dfrac{\kappa}{c}\)
where \(\kappa\) is the conductivity and \(c\) the concentration; with \(\kappa\) in S \(\mathrm{cm^{-1}}\) and \(c\) in mol \(\mathrm{L^{-1}}\) this becomes \(\Lambda_m = \dfrac{\kappa \times 1000}{c}\) in S \(\mathrm{cm^2\ mol^{-1}}\). (The marking scheme's sentence opens with the word "conductivity" but goes on to give the molar conductivity definition; the quantity defined is the molar one, as the phrase "containing one mole" shows.)

rows.stem:
(a) Write the hydrolysis products of lactose.
(b) What are non-essential amino acids ?
rows.solution:
(a) Lactose is a disaccharide of one glucose unit and one galactose unit joined by a \(\beta\)-1,4 glycosidic linkage, so hydrolysis gives D-(+)-glucose and D-(+)-galactose.

(b) Non-essential amino acids are those the body can synthesise for itself, so they need not be supplied ready-made in the diet. Glycine and alanine are examples. The ones the body cannot make — valine, leucine, lysine among them — are the essential amino acids.

rows.stem:
(a) Name two water-soluble vitamins.
(b) How will you prove the absence of free – CHO group in the cyclic structure of glucose molecule ?
rows.solution:
(a) Vitamin B and vitamin C. Both are water soluble, and being water soluble they are not stored in the body: any excess is excreted, so they must be supplied regularly in the diet.

(b) Convert glucose to its pentaacetate with acetic anhydride and then treat that with hydroxylamine. Hydroxylamine reacts with a free \(-\mathrm{CHO}\) group to give an oxime, and glucose pentaacetate does NOT react with it — so no free aldehyde group is present in that structure. Since all five hydroxyl groups have been acetylated and the aldehyde has still disappeared, the carbonyl carbon must have been tied up in a ring. This is one of the observations that established the cyclic hemiacetal structure of glucose.

rows.stem:
Calculate emf of the following cell at 298 K :
\(\mathrm{Al\,(s)} \mid \mathrm{Al^{3+}(aq)}\ (0{\cdot}1\ \mathrm{M}) \parallel \mathrm{Ni^{2+}(aq)}\ (0{\cdot}01\ \mathrm{M}) \mid \mathrm{Ni\,(s)}\)
(Given : \(\mathrm{E^{o}_{Ni^{2+}/Ni}} = -\,0{\cdot}25\) V, \(\mathrm{E^{o}_{Al^{3+}/Al}} = -\,1{\cdot}66\) V, [log 10 = 1])
rows.solution:
Aluminium is written on the left, so it is the anode and is oxidised; nickel is the cathode.
\(E^{\circ}_{cell} = E^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Ni^{2+}/Ni}} - E^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Al^{3+}/Al}} = (-0.25) - (-1.66) = 1.41\ \mathrm{V}\)

Balancing the electrons — aluminium gives up three each, nickel takes two each — the cell reaction is
\(2\mathrm{Al(s)} + 3\mathrm{Ni^{2+}(aq)} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{Al^{3+}(aq)} + 3\mathrm{Ni(s)}\)
so six electrons are transferred and \(n = 6\).

By the Nernst equation,
\(E_{cell} = E^{\circ}_{cell} - \dfrac{0.059}{6}\log\dfrac{[\mathrm{Al^{3+}}]^2}{[\mathrm{Ni^{2+}}]^3}\)
\(= 1.41 - \dfrac{0.059}{6}\log\dfrac{(10^{-1})^2}{(10^{-2})^3} = 1.41 - \dfrac{0.059}{6}\log 10^{4}\)
\(= 1.41 - \dfrac{0.059}{6} \times 4 = 1.41 - 0.039\)
\(= 1.371\ \mathrm{V}\)

The exponents come from the BALANCED cell reaction, not from the cell diagram, and \(n\) is 6 rather than 3 or 2 for the same reason.

rows.stem:
How do you convert the following ?
(a) Toluene to Benzaldehyde
(b) Benzoyl chloride to Acetophenone
(c) Bromobenzene to Benzoic acid
rows.solution:
(a) Toluene to benzaldehyde. Chromium trioxide in acetic anhydride oxidises the methyl group, but the anhydride traps the aldehyde as it forms as a gem-diacetate, which protects it from further oxidation; hydrolysis then releases the aldehyde.
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5CH_3} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{CrO_3}/(\mathrm{CH_3CO})_2\mathrm{O}} \mathrm{C_6H_5CH(OCOCH_3)_2} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{H_2O}} \mathrm{C_6H_5CHO}\)
The Etard reaction, with chromyl chloride followed by hydrolysis, achieves the same thing.

(b) Benzoyl chloride to acetophenone. A dialkyl cadmium is used rather than a Grignard reagent, because it is far less reactive and stops cleanly at the ketone instead of adding twice and giving a tertiary alcohol.
\(2\mathrm{C_6H_5COCl} + (\mathrm{CH_3})_2\mathrm{Cd} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{C_6H_5COCH_3} + \mathrm{CdCl_2}\)

(c) Bromobenzene to benzoic acid. Make the Grignard reagent, bubble in carbon dioxide, and acidify. The carbon of the carbon dioxide becomes the carboxyl carbon, so the product has one carbon more than the starting material.
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5Br} \xrightarrow[\text{dry ether}]{\mathrm{Mg}} \mathrm{C_6H_5MgBr} \xrightarrow[\text{(ii) }\mathrm{H^+}]{\text{(i) }\mathrm{CO_2}} \mathrm{C_6H_5COOH}\)

rows.subtopic: Temperature Dependence of the Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem:
The rate of a particular reaction quadruples when the temperature increases from 293 K to 313 K. Calculate the energy of activation \(\mathrm{(E_a)}\) of the reaction assuming that it does not change with temperature.
(Given : log 4 = \(0{\cdot}60\), R = \(8{\cdot}314\) \(\mathrm{JK^{-1}}\) \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\))
rows.solution:
Use the two-temperature form of the Arrhenius equation:
\(\log\dfrac{k_2}{k_1} = \dfrac{E_a}{2.303\,R}\left[\dfrac{T_2 - T_1}{T_1 T_2}\right]\)

The rate quadruples, so \(k_2/k_1 = 4\) and the left side is \(\log 4 = 0.60\). With \(T_1 = 293\) K and \(T_2 = 313\) K the bracket is \(\dfrac{20}{293 \times 313}\), so
\(0.60 = \dfrac{E_a}{2.303 \times 8.314} \times \dfrac{20}{293 \times 313} = \dfrac{E_a}{19.147} \times \dfrac{20}{293 \times 313}\)

\(E_a = \dfrac{0.60 \times 19.147 \times 293 \times 313}{20}\)
\(E_a = 52678.57\ \mathrm{J\ mol^{-1}}\), that is \(52.68\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\)

The unit is part of the answer; the marking scheme deducts half a mark if it is wrong or missing.

rows.stem:
(a) Write the IUPAC name of the given complex :
\(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_4(H_2O)Cl]\,Cl_2}\)
(b) Define polydentate ligand. Give an example.
(c) Mention the type of isomerism exhibited by the given complex :
\(\mathrm{[Co(en)_3]Cl_3}\)
rows.solution:
(a) Two chloride ions outside contribute \(-2\), so the complex cation is \(+2\). Inside it, four ammine and one aqua ligand are neutral and the chlorido ligand is \(-1\), which puts cobalt at \(+3\). Ligands are cited alphabetically — ammine, aqua, chlorido — so the name is tetraamineaquachloridocobalt(III) chloride.

(b) A polydentate ligand is one that binds the metal through SEVERAL donor atoms at once, occupying several coordination positions and closing one or more rings. EDTA, the ethylenediaminetetraacetate ion, is the standard example: it is hexadentate, gripping the metal through two nitrogen and four oxygen atoms.

(c) \(\mathrm{[Co(en)_3]Cl_3}\) exhibits optical isomerism. Three bidentate ethane-1,2-diamine ligands wrap round the cobalt in a propeller arrangement with no plane of symmetry, so the complex ion exists as two non-superimposable mirror images.

rows.stem:
(a) A coordination compound \(\mathrm{CrCl_3 \cdot 6H_2O}\) is mixed with excess of \(\mathrm{AgNO_3}\) solution, one mole of AgCl is precipitated per mole of the compound. Write the structural formula of the coordination compound.
(b) Write the oxidation state and hybridisation of the central metal in the given complex : \(\mathrm{[Fe(CN)_6]^{3-}}\). [Atomic number : Fe = 26]
(c) Why is \(\mathrm{[Ti(H_2O)_6]^{3+}}\) coloured ? [Atomic number : Ti = 22]
rows.solution:
(a) One mole of silver chloride per mole of compound means only ONE chloride is free in solution, so the other two must be inside the coordination sphere. With six positions to fill and two taken by chlorides, four water molecules complete the sphere, and the remaining two waters sit outside as water of crystallisation:
\(\mathrm{[Cr(H_2O)_4Cl_2]Cl \cdot 2H_2O}\)

(b) In \(\mathrm{[Fe(CN)_6]^{3-}}\) the six cyanido ligands contribute \(-6\) against an overall \(-3\), so iron is \(+3\) and \(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}\) is \(3d^5\). Cyanide is a strong field ligand, so it forces those five electrons to pair as far as they can into the lower set, leaving one unpaired and freeing two \(3d\) orbitals. Those two, with the \(4s\) and three \(4p\) orbitals, give the hybridisation \(d^2sp^3\) — an inner orbital octahedral complex, paramagnetic on account of the single unpaired electron.

(c) Titanium is \(+3\) here, so \(\mathrm{Ti^{3+}}\) is \(3d^1\) — a partly filled d subshell with one electron. The six water ligands split the d orbitals into two sets of different energy, and that single electron can absorb a photon of visible light to jump from the lower set to the upper one. This d-d transition removes part of the visible spectrum, and the complex appears in the complementary colour, purple. An ion with an empty or a completely filled d subshell has no such transition available and is colourless.
